prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at magic twist angles in twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle devices, opening the field of moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as a single-part prize with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. Round 1 sharpened rather than weakened the case. The discovery is a quantitative prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, with a specific magic angle and flat bands) followed seven years later by an observation that was not required by the prediction, correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. The result has been reproduced across many laboratories and carried to other moire platforms, and the twist angle is a single, directly measurable control parameter that turns interaction strength into a laboratory variable. As someone who works on statistical models, I find that last point the deepest part of the discovery. The citation can be written around the predicted flat bands and the observed phases and say nothing about the pairing mechanism, which answers the chair's first question on B047: the open mechanism is a follow-up question, not a maturity bar, because the prize criterion is a discovery and not a finished explanation. Olsson and Danielsson reached the same reading independently of me, and I find their arguments about checkability and breadth persuasive. On the chair's question about Bistritzer, I think his inclusion is warranted: the magic angle is a result of the 2011 calculation and the three-name limit lets the citation describe it accurately instead of crediting the idea to one author.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is maturity. B047 is about eight years old, the superconducting mechanism and several correlated phases are unresolved, and twist-angle disorder limits quantitative comparison with theory. Experimental credit is also concentrated: Cao, Fatemi and the parallel moire work of Dean and colleagues cannot be named under the three-person limit, and a prize would leave real contributions unrecognised. B012 is the more mature candidate, with more than fifteen years of independent confirmation, and it had broader opening support, with seven of eight members ranking it. If the committee decides that a settled interpretation is a requirement, B012 is the right choice and I would not oppose it. I have not moved to it because I do not think that requirement follows from the criterion, and because its attribution gap seems to me larger than the one for B047.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B012 as the candidate most colleagues can defend, arguing that the Z2 invariant and time-reversal-protected edge states are a separate discovery from the 2016 prize and that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are the clearest decisive-prediction-plus-first-observation trio available.
responses.response: I accept that the 2016 prize is context and not a bar: the Z2 classification and the observation in HgTe came later and were verified separately. Where I still differ is the attribution. The Nobel record does contain prizes that name the decisive prediction and the first observation and leave the wider community out, but here the experimental proposal that pointed to HgTe (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is itself outside the trio, and Zhang's death means it can never be repaired by a later prize. A citation that says 'observed in HgTe quantum wells' would credit an experiment whose theoretical trigger is unnamed. For B047 the prediction and the observation are both covered by the credited names, which is why I still rank it first. I also take your point that agreement on B012 is broad, and I would not treat my preference as a ruling; it is an argument about attribution, not about which field is more important.

responses.point: Eriksson judges B047 probably early, is comfortable with MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as the clean pair, treats Bistritzer as a defensible but not equally decisive third, and says that a few more years would make him more comfortable.
responses.response: The timing worry is the strongest argument against my choice and I do not dismiss it. I would answer that what is established is narrower than the pairing mechanism: flat bands near a magic angle, correlated insulators and superconducting domes, reproduced by independent groups, including with controlled variation of angle, filling and screening. High-Tc superconductivity was recognised long before its mechanism was understood. On Bistritzer, I disagree that he is a lesser third name. The 2011 paper is the origin of the specific angle and the flat-band structure; dropping him leaves MacDonald as the only theorist credited for a calculation they did together, and the two-name version describes the origin of the prediction less accurately. I do concede that a later year would reduce the risk, and that is a real cost of choosing now.

responses.point: Johansson, now preferring B012, argues that its physics has been settled for over a decade, that maturity should rank ahead of novelty, and that B047 should be revisited in a few years.
responses.response: I agree that maturity is a legitimate criterion and that B012 wins on it. Our disagreement is about weight. If the committee waits for settled interpretation in every case, it will systematically prefer fields where the discovery was followed by a long period of consolidation, and the committee's question about whether B047 could overtake B012 is partly answered by that asymmetry: B047 will not be less recognisable in three years, but the prediction-to-observation story is strongest now, while the names are all alive and active. I also note that your own text concedes the attribution gap in B012 and that you place B047 among your alternatives, so we are closer than the preferred configurations suggest. I would be content to see the committee discuss B012 first if its supporters can show a fair citation.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B047 first with Bistritzer included, ranks B012 second and doubts that B012's attribution is cleaner, and asks whether B012's broader opening support should discount B047.
responses.response: I agree with the configuration and with keeping Bistritzer. On the question of discounting, I do not think support counts should decide this: B012 was ranked by seven members but mostly second to fourth, and four members including you and me put B047 in the top three. Broad opening support tells us B012 is acceptable to nearly everyone, not that it is the strongest case. I want to qualify one point in your argument, though. You say B047 has the tidier chain, and I think that holds, but the three-name limit also leaves the first authors of the 2018 papers outside the prize, and I would not claim the attribution is clean, only that the gap is smaller and the credited names cover both the prediction and the key experiment.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature be checked before the citation wording is fixed, and is comfortable with a single experimental laureate because the 2018 pair of papers preceded the confirmations from other laboratories.
responses.response: I support the check and would make it a condition on the citation: earlier moire band-structure work (for example on twisted graphene layers and Dirac-cone velocity renormalisation by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) predates the 2011 paper and contributed the idea that twisting renormalises the bands. The citation should therefore say that the magic angle and the flat bands were predicted, not that moire effects were discovered. I have no evidence that this changes the credited set, but I cannot confirm it from the supplied material and want it flagged. I agree on the experimental side, where the first observation is clearly the Jarillo-Herrero group's 2018 pair of papers.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers the lattice clock (B019), arguing that its principle has been tested by independent groups for two decades with converging results and that a citation resting on the magic-wavelength lattice avoids a second-comb-prize reading.
responses.response: The distinction you draw between counting optical cycles (comb) and holding many atoms without perturbing the transition (lattice) is convincing, and it removes my concern about novelty against the 2005 prize. My remaining reservations are the scope of the new physics, which is a precision measurement achievement and not a new phenomenon, and the pending redefinition of the second. Those are judgments about breadth, not maturity or attribution, so I regard B019 as the strongest option on cleanliness and I keep it as an alternative. If the committee weights attribution and maturity over breadth, it is the right fallback.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a discovery prize for the flat bands and correlated phases while the superconducting mechanism is unresolved; this is the main reason a colleague could reasonably vote for B012 instead.
Whether the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature requires different wording or a different credited set; I have flagged it from memory and cannot check it from the supplied material.
Whether to credit Jarillo-Herrero alone on the experimental side when Cao, Fatemi and parallel moire work lie outside the three names.
Whether a fair Kane, Mele, Molenkamp citation for B012 can be drafted without reading as if the HgTe prediction were unattributed.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. His documented co-authors and institutions do not include any credited candidate on the shortlist. His research on active matter and stochastic processes is close in subject to B009 (field proximity, not a personal or institutional tie); B009 is no longer in his configuration or alternatives, so the disclosure is retained only for transparency. He has no documented tie to B047, B012 or B019.
